summary: Describes how to use the Authentication and Key Agreement (AKA) mechanism from mobile UMTS networks with HTTP Digest authentication. AKA is a challenge-response scheme based on symmetric cryptography, so this lets the same mobile credentials be used to log in over HTTP-style protocols such as SIP.

eli5.summary: Your phone company already has a secret handshake with your SIM card. This document lets that same handshake be used to prove who you are when a website or service asks.

subtitle: How to use the mobile-network AKA challenge-response as a one-time password for HTTP Digest and SIP logins.

tldr.problem: HTTP Digest authentication relies on a shared password, while UMTS mobile networks already authenticate users with the Authentication and Key Agreement (AKA) mechanism run on a tamper-resistant card.
tldr.mechanism: Digest AKA maps AKA parameters onto Digest: the server packs the AKA challenge (RAND and AUTN) into the nonce, and the client uses the AKA response (RES) as the Digest password.
tldr.outcome: AKA works as a one-time password generator for Digest, and the same approach applies to SIP and any other use of HTTP Digest. The memo is Informational and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 3310 is an Informational memo, and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It describes Digest AKA for HTTP Digest and SIP and builds on RFC 2617.

sections.title: Why Combine AKA and Digest
sections.content:
The HTTP Authentication Framework in RFC 2617 has two schemes, Basic and Digest. Both rely on a shared secret. Basic sends credentials in plain text. Digest hides them with cryptographic hashes and adds limited message integrity.

AKA (Authentication and Key Agreement) is the challenge-response mechanism that authenticates users in Universal Mobile Telecommunications System (UMTS) networks. It uses symmetric cryptography and is typically run in an ISIM, which sits on a smart-card-like device with tamper-resistant storage for shared secrets.

This memo maps AKA parameters onto Digest so that AKA acts as a one-time password generation mechanism. Because SIP authentication closely follows HTTP authentication, Digest AKA applies directly to SIP and to any other use of HTTP Digest.
sections.eli5: Phones already have a secret way to prove who they are to the phone company. This document lets that same trick be used on web-style logins instead of typing a password.

sections.title: How AKA Works
sections.content:
A secret K is set up beforehand and shared between the ISIM and the Authentication Center (AuC) of the home network. The AuC builds an authentication vector from K and a sequence number SQN. The vector holds a random challenge RAND, a network token AUTN, the expected result XRES, an integrity key IK and a cipher key CK. The server downloads one vector, or optionally a batch.

The server sends RAND and AUTN to the client. The ISIM checks AUTN using K and SQN. If it is valid, the network is authenticated and the client computes the response RES from K and RAND. The server compares RES with XRES. A match authenticates the user, and IK and CK can protect later traffic.

If the client finds the sequence numbers out of sync, it produces a synchronization parameter AUTS instead, and authentication is retried with vectors built from the re-synchronized number.
sections.eli5: The phone company sends a random puzzle plus a stamp proving it is the real phone company. The SIM solves the puzzle with its secret, and the answer is checked against the one the company expected.

sections.title: Digest AKA Directives
sections.content:
Digest AKA is identical to Digest in RFC 2617 except for a few extensions. The algorithm directive is overloaded: a value such as AKAv1-MD5 tells the client to use AKA instead of the standard password system. The default AKA version is AKAv1. If the directive is not understood, the nonce SHOULD be ignored and another challenge used if one is present. If the directive is absent, MD5 is assumed and AKA is not used.

The nonce carries the Base64 encoding of RAND, then AUTN, then optional server-specific data. The client extracts RAND and AUTN, checks AUTN and that the SQN is in the expected range, then runs AKA. The resulting RES is used as the password when calculating the Digest response.

If RES has limited entropy (the memo gives 32 bits as an example), it SHOULD be used only as a one-time password, and reuse is NOT RECOMMENDED. Algorithms such as MD5-sess SHOULD NOT be used with it.
sections.eli5: The login message says which kind of proof to use, and hides the puzzle inside a scrambled-looking code. The answer to the puzzle takes the place of the password.

sections.title: Resynchronization and Server Authentication
sections.content:
When the sequence number is out of sync, the client adds a new auts directive to its Authorization header, carrying the Base64 encoding of AUTS. In that case the client MUST calculate its credentials with an empty password. The server checks the AUTS value using K, uses a valid one to re-synchronize the SQN in the AuC, and re-challenges the client with a fresh vector.

AKA already authenticates the server through AUTN, but Digest's mutual authentication is still useful for message integrity. The server uses XRES as the password when calculating response-auth in the Authentication-Info header.

The memo walks through a successful SIP REGISTER exchange and a synchronization failure exchange.
sections.eli5: If the phone and the network have lost count of how many times they have talked, the phone sends a note saying so. The network fixes its count and asks again.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Digest AKA faces the same threats as HTTP authentication, with some differences. Because the long-term secret stays inside a tamper-resistant card and the card usually needs a PIN, neither possession of the host device nor Trojan Horses in its software reveal the secret. Digest AKA is typically more secure than regular Digest implementations.

Digest AKA passwords MUST NOT be re-used with schemes that send the password in clear, and in particular MUST NOT be re-used with HTTP Basic. A client given several algorithms MUST choose the strongest it understands, so AKAv1-MD5 beats MD5.

Dictionary attacks on passwords do not apply because the passwords come from the ISIM, but users should change the initial PIN. Sequence numbers give replay protection, and frequent sequence errors would reveal a cloned card. The cost is that servers must keep the current SQN for each user. The keys IK and CK are available, but the memo does not specify how to use them.
sections.eli5: The secret stays locked inside the SIM card, so even a hacked phone cannot read it. The main thing to watch is leaving the SIM's PIN on its factory setting.

sections.title: IANA Registry for AKA Versions
sections.content:
The memo creates an aka-version namespace coordinated by the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA). The default version is AKAv1, and versions above 1 are allocated by Expert Review.

A registration MUST include the version number with the AKAv prefix, so AKAv2 could be valid but FOOv2 or 2 would not be. It MUST also give contact information for the responsible party. The initial registry contains AKAv1.
sections.eli5: There is a list of numbered versions of the trick, kept by a central office. New versions must have the right name and a person to contact.
